body:
Eight defects found on the first hardware run of the rekey bench scenarios (D10S Plus r2240, v0.3.0-rc.6, macos-pkg channel).

The hardware work all succeeded. Two scenarios were scored FAILED by the harness rather than by the robot, which is what most of this fixes.

**bench scoring**
- `_ssh_public_fingerprint` required exactly 2 fields from `ssh-keygen -y`, but it prints the private key's comment as a third — and ssh-keygen defaults that comment to `user@host`. Every normal key failed, after the write had already landed.
- A newline queued during a long hardware step was consumed by the physical-observation prompt as its default. It can falsely fail a scenario, or falsely pass one nobody observed.

**AP identity**
- The AP wait settles for any SSH server, so on home Wi-Fi the serial-derived root password was offered to the router, and the post-write check reported a completed `flash misc` as the robot rejecting the key. Both now use Valetudo's `X-Valetudo-Version` header, the one identity probe that costs no credential. Proxy-bypassed, since an `http_proxy` would answer for a peer the ssh calls never reach.

**serial handling**
- A serial typed over the offered default and refused discarded the remembered value, sending the operator back under the robot for a label that was never wrong.
- A serial that authenticates proves whose `sn.txt` derived the password, so one that differs from the record now asks before writing. Confirming corrects the record — recon stores the label unconfirmed, so this cannot gate on the verified flag, and a hard stop would strand the rescue route.

**guidance**
- The over-ssh route printed the whole AP block twice.
- Prompts now say Enter accepts the offered value.
- Repeating the FEL sequence now notes the rail timer has usually booted the robot by then, which makes the button sequence silently do nothing.

1607 tests, ruff, strict mypy, release-scripts integration. Each commit reviewed by Codex; three rounds of its findings are folded in.
head: refs/pull/90/head
title: fix(rekey): first-contact defects from the session-3 bench

body:
ruff/mypy/pytest each live in three places that must agree exactly: the workflow literals CI installs with pip, `uv.lock` that `uv run` resolves, and pyproject.toml. pyproject held `>=` floors, which are permanently satisfied — so `pep621` raised nothing, only the annotated literals moved, and `test_pinned_toolchain_matches_the_lockfile` went red on every bump until someone ran `uv lock` by hand. ruff releases roughly weekly, so that was a standing chore (PR #89 was the latest instance).

Pinned exactly, pep621 raises the bump and relocks `uv.lock` as an artifact while the literals share the branch, so one PR carries all three. Green then proves the whole toolchain, which is what lets rule 27 drop `automerge: false` and fall through to the blanket patch/minor automerge.

**One assumption, deliberately left to be proven empirically:** Renovate has never updated a Python lockfile in any repo here, so its ability to run `uv lock` as an artifact update is untested. The failure mode if it cannot is identical to today — the equality test goes red and the PR waits, with the `uv lock` fallback still printed in `prBodyNotes` — plus a dependency-dashboard artifact error. So this is safe to try, and the next ruff release settles it.

Also fixes a tautological assertion Codex caught in the first draft: it compared two constants declared in the same file and would not have noticed `automerge: false` coming back. It now reads `.renovaterc.json`, and was verified to fail when a hold is re-added.

1607 tests, ruff, strict mypy, `uv lock --check`. Versions unchanged by the relock (ruff 0.16.2, mypy 2.3.0, pytest 9.1.1); only the recorded specifiers move.

body:
Eight deps were held off automerge. Every one of them for the same reason: something bound to the version — a digest with no datasource, a lockfile — could not move with it, so the branch arrived half-applied and someone had to finish it by hand.

`packaging/refresh-pins.sh` recomputes all of them from whatever version Renovate just wrote, as a `postUpgradeTask`, so the branch is complete before CI sees it:

- `VALETUDO_SHA256` — all three per-arch release assets, including the version comment beside each
- `BUNDLE_PYTHON_SHA256` — from the `.tar.xz` `deb.Dockerfile` actually compiles, not the `.tgz`
- `TMUX_SHA256` — from the release tarball the `.pkg` builds
- `depends_on "python@3.x"` in both Homebrew formulae, which no Renovate manager reads

Written for the Renovate container as much as for a developer: no `python3` (that image is Node-based), no GNU-only sed flags, both sha256 spellings. It refuses to write a digest it could not download, and is idempotent — verified by running it against the current tree, where it recomputed all five digests from upstream and produced no diff, then by bumping CPython to 3.14.7 and watching it derive the new checksum unaided.

All eight `automerge: false` holds are gone. Rules that existed only to carry a hold are deleted; the ones with real information keep it.

Tests now assert the inverse invariant: no rule holds anything, and **every** `*_SHA256` bound to a version is named by the refresher — so adding a new digest pin without teaching it about that pin fails, rather than quietly reintroducing the chore. The two static digests with no upstream feed (`STAGE1_SHA256`, `DUST_KEYSTREAM_SHA256`) are exempt by name with the reason.

Requires the matching `RENOVATE_ALLOWED_POST_UPGRADE_COMMANDS` allowlist on the self-hosted instance (bryantserver/k8s), anchored to this one script.

**One judgement call worth seeing:** `sunxi-tools` tracks a raw upstream *commit*, not a release, and is compiled into every build that talks to the robot's boot ROM. It needed no hand-editing, so its hold is gone too — but that means upstream commits now reach a release without anyone reading them. Its test was rewritten to assert what still holds: the pin is a full 40-hex commit, never a floating ref.

1608 tests, ruff, strict mypy, shellcheck.

PRs #92 and #93 both went red on `CI / macos` while GitHub's `ci-macos` had already **passed** for their exact head SHAs.

Timing rules out the obvious explanations. GitHub's runs finished at 15:34:10 and 15:40:20 UTC; the Forgejo bridge jobs did not start until 15:48:51 and 15:49:19. The successful run was already sitting there when the bridge began. The macOS job then ran for about 2m49s — the script's 180s `initial_delay` plus a single API call.

So it never got an answer: `curl -fsSL` under `set -e` aborts the whole script on any non-2xx, and the job dies. Near-certainly a 403 on the runners' shared egress IP, whose 60 unauthenticated requests/hour the script's own comment budgets for "two concurrent gates" — today ran far more than two.

The consequence is the bad part: a busy hour reddens every gate in flight simultaneously, reporting a macOS verdict GitHub never gave, and only a human can clear it.

Now an unreachable API spends an attempt and asks again. Fail-closed is unchanged — a `completed` run with a non-success conclusion still fails immediately, and exhausting the budget still fails.

Two cases added to the existing fake-curl harness: `ratelimited` (first call fails, then success — must pass) and `unreachable` (every call fails — must still fail, not silently pass). Verified against the unfixed script, where the suite exits **22**, curl's own error code, which is exactly what production did.

1608 tests, shellcheck, both integration suites.

Each install scenario required the Valetudo marker to be absent at the start and present at the end, so the first one to run permanently closed the other five on that robot. A campaign could never qualify the full install path.

Found at the bench on 2026-08-09, mid-campaign, while planning full coverage of 0.3.0-rc.8.

- Repeats are allowed; `push()` already publishes a fresh factory-backup generation every run and has no already-installed short circuit.
- A repeat is refused only when it would downgrade the robot. `push()` replaces the executable unconditionally while only `update_valetudo()` compares versions, so `valetudo_would_downgrade` now gates it. That hole predates this change: the absent-marker gate never protected against it, since a robot can run a newer Valetudo while carrying no marker at all.
- `bench report` marks a repeat as `(reinstall, not a first install)` so it cannot be mistaken for first-install coverage.

Offline reachability analysis over the readiness state machine puts 31 of 32 automated scenarios in reach across two workspaces. The remaining one, `reroot-after-restore`, needs a completed stock restore and is hardware-blocked.

1621 tests, ruff, strict mypy green. The new regression tests were confirmed to fail against the unfixed code.

body:
`push` and `backup` could not complete on any robot. Three gates required `/mnt/private/ULI/factory/config.txt`: the live identity read, the archive member check, and the traceability check. No Dreame robot has that file.

Evidence, not inference:

- A live D10s Plus (r2240) factory directory lists `cpuid.txt`, `did.txt`, `key.txt`, `language.txt`, `mac.txt`, `nation.txt`, `sn.txt`, `timezone.txt` — no `config.txt`.
- A captured X40 Ultra (r2416) backup has the same set plus Matter certs, also no `config.txt`.
- That robot's config value appears in none of its files, nor in its raw `private.dd` or `misc.dd`. The config is a `fastboot getvar` answer and lives only in the bootloader.
- `private` is not among the partitions `root` writes, so its contents are factory-original: if a rooted robot lacks the file, a stock one does too.

Why no test caught it: the fixtures scripted the robot's reply as `factory_config=config: <hex>`, which real hardware cannot produce. The Runner seam proves which commands are sent, not that the robot answers as a fixture claims.

The replacement anchor is the SoC id, which every real robot carries and every backup preserves. Nothing knows it in advance — recon reads the bootloader and its capture stops short of `private` — so it is pinned on first contact, gated behind a matching recorded serial or an explicit operator confirmation, and only after the model check so a rejected robot cannot bind the workspace. Thereafter it must match exactly.

Verified against real robot bytes: the X40 archive the old code rejected now passes `_tar_has_factory_data`, its cpuid reads clean, and a wrong robot is still refused. 1628 tests, ruff, strict mypy green; three rounds of Codex review, final pass clean.

title: fix(push): bind a robot by the SoC id it actually carries

body:
Found by running the campaign on hardware. Three of twelve scenarios failed; none was operator error.

**fix-impl reported the UI down while it was up.** The readiness probe was `curl -sf`, and `-f` fails on any HTTP >= 400. A Valetudo with authentication on answers 401 until you log in, so the probe could never succeed: the log shows `rc=22` for 37 straight seconds while Valetudo was demonstrably alive. It now uses `valetudo_version_header`, the credential-free probe the F2 fix already added, which also proves it is Valetudo replying.

**The two interruption scenarios were unsatisfiable by hand.** The whole factory backup lands in about 0.9s on a D10s Plus (`+0.9s` to `+1.8s` in the transcript); the binary copy takes ~27s. Asking an operator to pull Wi-Fi or press Ctrl+C during the backup means every attempt arrives after it finished, so both failed a robot that behaved correctly. A second defect compounded it: a drop during the transfer raised a message outside the three the scenario tolerated, so its own reconnect-and-retry never ran.

The conductor now injects the interruption at the Runner seam, at each point an install can be lost: the three backup pulls, the deviceId and miio-key repairs, the binary copy, and the atomic rename. Every command before the trigger runs for real, so it is still the production phase against real hardware, and each point is judged on its own terms rather than a blanket rule.

Each point guards on all the points after it. Without that, a boundary this robot skips would let push() run on through a real install and reboot while the conductor waited for a trigger that cannot come, and an earlier sweep passing through a one-shot repair would leave the next sweep nothing to interrupt. Guards are derived from the sweep order rather than hand-listed, because a hand-listed one already got that wrong once.

Nine rounds of Codex review; every finding either applied or answered. One was declined on the merits: arming the tar boundary only after production's archive validation is not reachable from a seam that sits at command boundaries, and the sweep's claim is that interrupting there is clean, not that the archive was good. The triggering exit code is recorded per point instead, so a reader can see it.

1633 tests, ruff, strict mypy green.

body:
Two hardware-bench scenarios could not be passed by a healthy robot.

**`implementation-fix`** ended with "Does the Valetudo web interface now load with the correct robot implementation?" Valetudo does not display its implementation class anywhere, and a password-protected instance shows a login form before it shows anything, so the question had no honest answer either way. It failed on the rc.10 campaign for exactly this reason. The pin is a value in a file on the robot, so the scenario now reads that file back and compares it against the live model.

The derivation moved into `resolved_impl_class` in `phases/fixes.py` and is shared with the phase, so the check cannot certify a class `fix-impl` would not have written.

**`rekey-over-usb`** ends in a fastboot reboot, then calls `_confirm_authorized_key`, which waits `_AP_IDENTITY_POLLS * _AP_IDENTITY_SECONDS` = 45s for the robot to answer on its AP. That budget was sized for `/mnt` finishing its mount, not for a boot plus an operator starting the AP and joining it — so a key the robot had accepted would be recorded as refused. It now pauses for the operator first. The SSH route reboots nothing and is unchanged.

Found while writing the Block 6-7 (USB/FEL) driver for the rc.12 bench campaign.

- 1640 Python tests pass; ruff and mypy clean
- new coverage: pin read-back pass/fail, live-model mismatch, not-the-robot address, and the USB/SSH/unattended rekey routes
- `docs/HARDWARE-TESTING.md` expectation column updated
- also merges the duplicate `### Added` heading under `[Unreleased]`

body:
Everything the rc.12 bench session turned up, plus the conductor that keeps it from happening again.

**Product defects**

- A Homebrew install resolved pyusb from PyPI on every fastboot call. That fails on the robot own AP, which has no internet and is exactly where the install runs. The formulae now vendor the pinned pyusb into their virtualenv, the transport prefers an interpreter carrying that exact version, and a failure that is really the network says so instead of blaming libusb.
- Answering "continue?" after a failed command ran the auto chain rather than the command that failed, then reported every phase complete.
- rekey over USB announced a reboot it never confirmed (the request is unacknowledged, and a FEL-booted robot often stays off), then judged the key against whatever answered 192.168.5.1 — the router, on a home network.

**Bench**

- `bench campaign` runs a whole session: it re-reads what the robot can qualify before each scenario, says what to do and what to answer first, waits for the robot rather than for any responder, and explains every skip.
- It schedules in passes so a write cannot strand the scenarios that needed the state it took, and asks before spending a one-time boundary.
- `usb-drop-recon` is gated to a robot with no write history — recon skips the recovery pull otherwise, so it had no transfer to interrupt and failed a healthy robot. Restoring to stock does not reopen it.
- `rekey-over-usb` is judged on the key it authorized, not on a reboot nobody confirmed.

rc.13 built its tag but lost every Linux asset. The arm64 `.deb` is built and smoke-tested inside BuildKit QEMU, and PyInstaller 6.22.0 added a onefile bootloader check (GHSA-9fxf-4qw3-ghmr) that 6.22.1 activated on POSIX: a onefile child requires its parent to be running the same executable. Under emulation the parent is `/dev/.buildkit_qemu_emulator`, so every frozen binary refuses to start — the build-time smoke, the packaged `version` check, and `bench run host-smoke` alike.

ci.yml builds amd64 only, so nothing before release time can see this. Tolerating the error was the alternative and it would have retired the one pre-release check that runs the arm64 package at all, so the pin goes back instead.

SisyphusMD/whiskerless hit this first and holds the same version; its `packaging/check-pyinstaller-pin.sh` documents when the pin can be lifted. The Renovate clamp here is scoped to the two Forgejo workflows, because release-macos.yml freezes natively and is unaffected.

body:
Lifts the PyInstaller hold by removing the thing that broke, not by waiving it.

**Why rc.13 lost its Linux assets.** 6.22.0 added a onefile bootloader check for
GHSA-9fxf-4qw3-ghmr and 6.22.1 activated it on POSIX: a onefile child requires its parent to be
running the same executable. Inside BuildKit's QEMU emulation the kernel reports
`/dev/.buildkit_qemu_emulator`, so every frozen binary the arm64 leg produced refused to start.

**Why onedir settles it.** The check is called only from the onefile branch of upstream's
`pyi_main.c`; onedir spawns no child, so it never runs. `pyi_security.c` has no opt-out, only a
skip for an unreadable `/proc/<ppid>` — verified against v6.22.2 source, not inferred.

- `BUNDLE_MODE` parameterises both build scripts and defaults to **onefile**; `deb.Dockerfile` is
  the only caller passing `onedir`, so `release-macos.yml` keeps signing a single file. A contract
  test pins that default, since ordinary macOS CI never assembles the `.pkg`.
- Each Linux tool installs as its own tree (`/usr/lib/dreame-valetudo/{app,fastboot}`) reached
  through a symlink — `find_helper` needs a runnable file at
  `/usr/lib/dreame-valetudo/dreame-fastboot`, and the bootloader resolves symlinks before looking
  for its contents directory.
- `packaging/check-package-parity.py` compares each installed tree against the built tree, entry
  types included. nfpm assembles the package outside the build image, so nothing else in the
  release path would notice a bundle that silently lost `libexec/dustbuilder-forms`.
- Both bench fingerprints now cover whole trees. A onedir launcher is a near-generic stub; hashing
  it alone would let two different builds share one campaign and merge their hardware results.
- `packaging/nfpm-legacy-layout.yaml` reproduces the pre-onedir installed shape as the starting
  point of an upgrade case. Every other case upgrades one current-layout package to another, so
  nothing else exercises the transition users take.
- The clamp is gone from `.renovaterc.json`; all three workflows float at 6.22.2 together again.

**Verified off-CI**, per the repo's own rule about `packaging/` changes. A real `linux/arm64`
`deb.Dockerfile` build produced both bundles, smoke-ran its own launchers, and passed the glibc
floor check walking the trees. The pinned nfpm preserved tree symlinks and modes; the parity check
matched 75 and 85 entries against a real `.deb`. `test-linux-packages.sh` then ran the full smoke
in a Debian container over that package: pre-onedir fixture -> upgrade -> layout, bundled data,
`version`, `bench run host-smoke`, fastboot client load -> uninstall with both trees removed and
the test backup preserved. Separately, mutating one file inside `_internal` of a real bundle
invalidates a bench campaign while the launcher stays byte-identical.

**Still open, deliberately.** Native arm64 verification (the durable answer — emulation is a proxy
for the artifact that ships), and the rc that actually settles the lift. `whiskerless` is NOT
getting this fix: it publishes raw single-file executables, so onedir would mean redesigning its
asset contract.

body:
Twelve defects found running a real 0.3.0-rc.15 campaign on the D10S Plus bench robot.

## Scenarios no healthy robot could pass

- **`wrong-model-root`** returned early for an adopted or already-rooted robot, *above* the recon-model gate it exists to qualify, so it recorded "completed normally instead of producing the expected safe stop" on every robot past its first flash. It now probes with `force=True`; the model gate is not force-gated and dies before `doctor()`, `image()` and the first runner call, so the probe reaches the gate under test and stays fail-closed. The old test stubbed `root`, which is why the ordering defect survived — the new one calls the real thing.
- **The restore family** read READY from state markers alone. This robot carries no `restored-stock`, `flash-attempt` or `restore-attempt`, while what restore actually needs — a capture attested as untouched factory firmware — appeared in no marker map. The conductor offered to spend `research-baseline`, `terminal-loss-restore` and `ssh-wrong-key` buying a scenario `restore.py` refuses at its own gate. Eligibility now consults the provenance record, tri-state so that an absent record is not a refusal (restore attests a legacy capture interactively) and a kit this robot already has overrides it (restore returns that without reading provenance).

## Answer what the conductor already knows

New `Console.answering(Answer)` seam. The conductor pre-answers questions the **real** production phases raise — no `--yes` flags, no stubs — echoes each with the reason it was settled, and records them in `report.json` under `answered_automatically`. An answer that arrives silently is indistinguishable from a person having given it.

Settled: both recon adoption questions, the recon re-run offer, and the serial prompt — with a derived wrong serial fed first for `rekey-wrong-serial`. Rekey scenarios generate a key per run under `robots/<id>/bench-keys/`, novel by construction, retiring a fixed pool that `replace()` consumes one write at a time. `DREAME_SSHKEY` still wins if set.

**Never settled, pinned by a test against the literal prompts:** the stock-firmware attestation, the brick-risk accept, the pre-write confirmations, the robot-identity checks, and the H3 arming phrase.

## Tell the operator where to be

Every surface is announced, not just the cable one, and a change of surface names the step between the two — including that a scenario ending in fastboot leaves the robot unable to serve its AP until power-cycled. The banner now precedes the surface waits, so nobody is asked to move before knowing why, and rival/contested decisions are taken before that so no setup is wasted. The Enter gate fires only where a person must act and nothing polls for it. Eligible work is re-picked to finish a surface before leaving it. Progress reports `[n/m]` plus a running tally. `DREAME_NO_BROWSER` stops a browser taking the terminal mid-scenario. The arming prompt now says why it is asked — and is deliberately still required for the scenarios that refuse before opening the USB device, because the refusal is the thing under test.

## Verification

1728 tests, ruff, strict mypy, shellcheck, release-scripts integration all green locally. `bench plan` against the real D10S workspace now reports the three restore scenarios WAIT with the reason and `wrong-model-root` READY.

Codex cold review caught one P1 before it shipped: `legacy-root-adoption` forbids the `rooted` marker in its starting contract — the robot was rooted before this tool existed — so a marker-derived answer denied the scenario's own premise and left `root-origin` unset. Same unpassable class as the two above. Fixed and pinned.

body:
Converges the release pipeline with whiskerless and removes every trace of QEMU emulation.

**Architecture decides the forge, and nothing is emulated.** amd64 builds and install-tests on the
Forgejo runner; arm64 and macOS on GitHub's native runners, via the same
`build-linux-arch.sh`/`install-matrix-arch.sh` both projects now share. Adds the GitHub install
matrix this repo never had (macOS `.pkg`, bottle pour, PyPI, plus the arm64 Linux legs).

**Release-path fixes found by a cold cross-repo audit:**

- **a stable could be cut with a red install matrix** — the workflow claimed the matrix gated the
  next stable and nothing read its result; there is now a `candidate-gate`
- `publish.yml` had no manual redrive, so any late transient failure cost another tag; it is now
  dispatchable behind a tag-grammar guard
- jobs carrying `always()`/`!cancelled()` ran even when that guard *refused* the ref
- the rc sweep never touched the apt/dnf repositories, so superseded rc packages were served
  forever; it now prunes them, gated on the stable actually replacing them in the same
  distributions and architectures
- an unreadable registry was reported as "not published", which is a different claim
- the published `.rpm` was never install-tested on openSUSE at all

Every `setup-python` call now carries the retry the rest of the pipeline already used.

**Do not cut a release from `main` until this lands:** the signing key and `.repo` files the
install channels fetch exist only on this branch.

head: refs/pull/124/head
title: Give the tap job its own Python, and clamp the two unguarded floors

body:
Homebrew refuses to LOAD a formula from an untrusted third-party tap. Building the rc bottle loads the stable formula too, because the rc formula's `conflicts_with` names it.

That means this only bites once a stable formula exists in the tap. dreame-valetudo has one, so every bottle job on rc.17 and rc.18 died with `Refusing to load formula ... from untrusted tap`. whiskerless has no stable formula in the tap yet, so it was passing on an absence rather than on correctness — and would have broken the first time 0.2.0 shipped.

Guarded on the subcommand existing, not on its exit status: an older Homebrew has no `trust` and needs none, while a `trust` that exists and fails is a real problem and must stop the build.

Ports the CONDITION, not just the endpoint: sending every install to the enumerating URL would offer stable users a prerelease their upgrade command cannot install.

body:
The same rockylinux:9 image carried two depNames — `rocky-9-compat` in ci.yml, `rocky-9-current` in install-smoke.Dockerfile — and only the first was clamped, so Renovate retried a bump to Rocky 10 forever. whiskerless names it `rocky-9-compat` in the same file.

Converges the Renovate surface onto whiskerless shape: one custom manager owns every packaging Dockerfile (globbed, not named file by file), the built-in dockerfile manager is off rather than disabled per file, and `homebrew/brew` is annotated like its sibling.

Also fixes a live drift the old invariant could not see: it compared the toolchain pin in one workflow, so a ruff bump reached the Forgejo workflows, pyproject.toml and uv.lock while GitHub PR lint stayed on 0.16.3. It now compares all five workflows and all five tools.

body:
A candidate died on `curl: (6) Could not resolve host: astral.sh` while fetching the uv installer. The infra-retry workflow correctly declined to rescue it — the failure was inside one of our own steps, which is exactly what that workflow refuses to launder into green. So the fix belongs on the fetch.

- every network fetch in the install path now retries
- the installer is written to a file, never piped: curl cannot rewind a pipe, so a retried partial body would reach `sh` concatenated with the first
- container fetches retry in the shell via `packaging/fetch.sh`, because `--retry` alone does not cover a name-resolution failure and Rocky 8 ships curl 7.61, which rejects `--retry-all-errors` outright

rc.43 died on `dist/whiskerless: A timestamp was expected but was not found` while signing the x86_64 pkg. arm64 signed fine on the same run, so it was a transient outage at Apple.

Every macOS release step reaches an Apple service on every invocation: `codesign` and `productsign` each request a trusted timestamp, `notarytool` uploads, and `stapler` downloads the ticket back. All four now go through `packaging/retry.sh` with a backoff that spans two and a half minutes.

Dropping the timestamp was never an option - it is what keeps the signature verifiable past the certificate expiry, and notarization refuses a build without one.

The invariant derives the covered window from the script and the workflow rather than restating it, so widening one without the other cannot pass quietly.

body:
A workflow-shape audit across all 14 shared workflows, after an earlier convergence pass checked Renovate identities, action pins and install channels but never looked at triggers or concurrency.

Three divergences, each repo missing something the other had:

- `.forgejo/ci.yml` had `workflow_dispatch` in whiskerless only. Forgejo has no rerun API, so dreame main was stranded red by a cluster-wide network outage with no way back except an unrelated commit.
- `.forgejo/ci.yml` had per-ref concurrency in whiskerless only, so dreame left superseded runs competing for runners.
- `.forgejo/publish.yml` had per-tag serialisation in dreame only, so whiskerless publishing was not deduplicated at all.

Both publish groups now key on the FULL ref: `ref_name` drops refs/heads and refs/tags alike, so a branch sharing a tag name would share its group, and publish.yml is dispatchable.

Guards mirrored into both, each mutation-verified.
head: refs/pull/136/head
title: Converge the workflow shape: dispatch and concurrency

body:
Re-lands the bottle mirroring reverted earlier, with the reason it was reverted actually fixed.

Setting `HOMEBREW_ARTIFACT_DOMAIN` makes Homebrew suppress the anonymous `Authorization: Bearer QQ==` it would otherwise send to ghcr.io, so any bottle the mirror could not serve fell back bare and got a 401. `HOMEBREW_DOCKER_REGISTRY_TOKEN=QQ==` restores exactly that anonymous credential: ghcr.io answers 200 for it (verified directly) and the mirror ignores it, so a mirror miss downloads the bottle instead of failing the job.

Measured from a runner rather than a workstation: a cold entry syncs in about 21s against the roughly 7s Homebrew's default three retries allow, which is what the raised retry budget is for; a 170MB bottle already synced serves in about 2s. The repo invariant now fails if either the credential or the retry budget is dropped while a mirror is set.
head: refs/pull/137/head
title: Mirror Homebrew bottles again, with the ghcr fallback credential restored

body:
Closes a divergence that was never recorded: whiskerless has `.github/workflows/formula-macos.yml` and dreame had no counterpart.

My first attempt was to record this as *intended*, on the grounds that dreame declares `dependencies = []` and so has no native code to mis-link. That was wrong, and a cold review caught it: the **formula** compiles C regardless of what pyproject says. `dreame-valetudo.rb` stages the `sunxi-tools` resource and builds it with `make sunxi-fel` against libfdt and zlib, and depends on `libusb`, `dtc`, `zlib` and `pkg-config`. A macOS-only compile or link failure was reachable there and nowhere else before a tag existed.

Also wires it into the two places a new workflow has to be registered: the `retry-infra-failures` list, and both release gates, which now require the formula check and the CI matrix rather than the matrix alone.

**Known limit, stated in the workflow:** one `macos-26` lane, so an Intel-only or macOS-floor-only native break still reaches a tag. Whiskerless's job has the same single lane; widening both to the full matrix triples the most expensive runners on every push and is a cost decision, not a fix to slip in here.
head: refs/pull/138/head
title: Build the Homebrew formula on macOS before tagging

body:
The mirror syncs **on demand**, so the first request for a bottle it has never seen blocks while it pulls from ghcr.io — measured at about 21s per entry from a runner, against the roughly 7s Homebrew's default three retries allow. The smoke jobs raise that budget so a cold entry survives, but it is paid again on every dependency whenever upstream rebuilds its bottles.

This walks the formula's own dependency closure with `brew deps` and fetches each bottle with `brew fetch`, which is what populates the mirror. Nothing hardcodes a formula list that could drift from what the smoke installs.

**Verified on a real runner, not asserted:** whiskerless warms 62/62 of its closure and dreame 85/85, both with zero misses.

Three things a cold review caught, each fixed and then re-tested:

- `HOMEBREW_ARTIFACT_DOMAIN_NO_FALLBACK` is set **here only**. Without it every fetch could succeed from ghcr.io and report a warm mirror that received nothing. The smoke jobs deliberately keep the fallback, where a miss should cost latency rather than a red build.
- The **rc** formula is warmed first, and chosen by which file exists rather than by an exit code. `update-tap.sh` advances only the rc on a prerelease, so the stable formula lags — measured three dependencies short of its own rc in dreame.
- `brew trust` is applied as the install smoke does; without it, reading a third-party formula exits non-zero even when it printed the formula correctly, which silently selected the stale closure.

**Known limit, stated in the workflow:** the closure comes from the published tap, so a dependency newly added to the local formula template is not warm until a release publishes it. The first job to want it pays one cold sync, which the raised retry budget already absorbs.
head: refs/pull/139/head
title: Warm the bottle mirror daily

body:
The formula job proved current arm64 and nothing else, while `ci-macos.yml` holds the library to four lanes. Both formulae compile native code on the installing machine — a Rust extension in whiskerless, `sunxi-tools` built with `make sunxi-fel` here — so a break can be specific to Intel or to the macOS floor. The bottle build does cover those lanes, but only at tag time, and a tag is immutable by the time it reports.

Four lanes of a job that compiles is not cheap. Killing this workflow's duplicate `pull_request` run earlier paid for half of it; the rest buys the only coverage that was missing.

A new invariant fails if the two lane sets ever diverge again, in either direction.
head: refs/pull/140/head
title: Build the formula on every macOS lane the library is tested on

body:
Two fixes to the gate this repo already had.

**It ran unauthenticated.** Unauthenticated GitHub allows 60 requests an hour per IP, shared with everything else leaving this network — including whiskerless's copy of the same gate, now that it has one, polling the same API for the same reason. Exhausting it turns the gate into a timeout that blames the mirror for a commit nothing was wrong with. The token needs no scopes for a public repo.

An invariant here previously asserted `"secrets." not in` the job. That pinned a spelling, not a property: `prerelease.yml` passes this same read-only token on this same runner, and its comment states the property that matters is holding no WRITE credential. The test now asserts that instead, case-insensitively.

**Its checkout persisted credentials**, leaving the repository token in git config while a script from a PR-controlled ref runs beside it. Now `persist-credentials: false`.

body:
whiskerless has shipped `SHA256SUMS-x86_64` and `SHA256SUMS-aarch64` since backlog #75; this repo shipped none, so anyone downloading a `.deb`, `.rpm` or tarball from a release page had no integrity check at all. `dpkg -i` verifies nothing and `rpm -i` only warns if configured.

This is **not** a replacement for signing. The packages are GPG-signed and apt/dnf verify that automatically from the repository channel — that proves origin. Checksums answer the different question, *did this arrive intact*, for the direct-download path where nothing checks anything.

Three review findings fixed along the way:

- **Historical dispatches would have broken.** Adding the roles made `wait-for-release.sh` require them for every tag, and both install matrices deliberately support dispatching current scripts against an older tag — every pre-checksum release would have waited out 120 polls and failed. There is now an explicit optional-role concept: reconcile still heals them, completeness does not block.
- **The NAS bridge count** was still 5 against six selectors, so it could have called an incomplete mirror complete.
- **The source tarball** is arch-independent but hashed into the x86_64 manifest, since that is the machine that builds it; the comment now says so rather than implying `uname -m` covers it.

Reconcile treats a missing role as a warning, so existing releases (which have no checksums) warn rather than fail — honest, since they genuinely lack them.
head: refs/pull/145/head
title: Publish per-architecture SHA256SUMS for the Linux artifacts

body:
`v0.3.0-rc.27` lost its bottles, and the install matrix that waits on them, to a **sixty-second** miss.

`build-bottles.sh` waits for publish.yml's first tap pass; publish.yml's second pass then waits for the bottles built here. That handshake is correct and unchanged. What failed was the budget: `90 x 20s` = **30 minutes**, against a publish that took **37m18s** to write the formula (started 16:45:56Z, tap pass landed 17:23:12Z). The loop gave up at 17:22:12Z. The formula appeared one minute later.

The same publish has reached the tap inside 17 minutes on other runs, so the spread is wide and 30 minutes sat inside it. Now `270 x 20s` = 90 minutes.

**Widening is close to free.** The loop breaks the moment the formula appears, so the budget is a FAILURE bound rather than a delay: it costs nothing on a healthy release and a longer red run when publishing is genuinely broken.

**This applies to stable too.** `bottles.yml` triggers on `v*.*.*`, so `v0.3.0` races exactly as the rc did — and stable's publish does more before the tap pass, while a stable tag is permanent. `retry-infra-failures` would not have saved it either: it re-runs *infrastructure* failures, and `::error::the tap never published…` is an application-level failure it correctly declines.

A new invariant fails if the budget drops under 60 minutes, mutation-tested against both factors — fewer iterations and a shorter sleep. The failure message now names the recovery dispatch.

body:
A dropped connection to one forge failed a whole release leg. Three things turned that transient into a terminal error:

- `rel_asset_state` returned `1` both for "the request failed" and for "the metadata is unreadable", so a reset was indistinguishable from a real byte conflict. It now returns `12` for a failed request.
- `rel_verify_uploaded_asset` retried `10` (not visible yet) but returned immediately on `1`. That is what actually failed the last bottle publish: the upload succeeded, the *verify read* was reset, and a failed lookup was treated as a verdict. It now keeps looking on `12`.
- Uploads had no retry at all. `rel_upload_verified` now retries, and re-checks forge state before every attempt, so a write that landed before the connection broke is recognised rather than repeated. No upload is issued without a definite ABSENT verdict.

Retried reads are also written to a file curl can truncate rather than a stdout it cannot rewind, so a body reset mid-response cannot be concatenated with its replacement and parsed as malformed JSON.

`REL_MUTATE` still carries no curl-level retry, which stays correct: curl cannot tell a write that never landed from one that landed and lost its reply. The retry belongs one level up, where it can look first.

Vendored from project-standard v0.1.17. Covered by six new unit tests (each mutation-tested) and the existing release integration suite on both forges.

body:
A mirror that drops a connection mid-fetch is not this project failing, but apt treats it as fatal and the whole install leg goes red for it — observed on `ports.ubuntu.com` during the rc.48 arm64 matrix, where `deb-file-ubuntu` and `deb-file-ubuntu-floor` both died on `Failed to fetch`.

Retries are set as apt POLICY (`Acquire::Retries "3"` in `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/`) in every stage that runs `apt-get update`, so all derived stages inherit it and a new leg cannot forget.

Deliberately NOT done by widening `triage-infra-failure.py`: that script only treats runner-phase failures as infrastructure, and its own reasoning is that broadening it would become a way to launder flaky tests into green builds. Making the fetch survive the network is a different thing from excusing a failure — a package that genuinely does not install still fails.

Verified in a real ubuntu:22.04 arm64 container (`apt-config dump` shows the policy active, install succeeds). The new invariant asserts no `apt-get update` exists without the policy, and refuses to pass if its own scan finds nothing.
head: refs/pull/151/head
title: Let apt retry a dropped mirror fetch

body:
Two changes, one per commit.

**The install matrix no longer races the publish it depends on.** It triggered on the tag push — the same instant `publish.yml` starts — so its wait job held one of the runner's few slots for its whole budget, polling for artifacts the publish it was starving had not built yet. Measured on the sibling: ~14 minutes of real publish work stretched to 50, with 15- and 21-minute gaps where no publish job ran at all. Forgejo has no `workflow_run`, so the finished publish now hands off explicitly. It runs even when a producer failed, deliberately: `reconcile` can heal a partly-failed release, and under default `needs` semantics that healed, COMPLETE release would have had its handoff skipped — a release with no install matrix at all.

**The .rpm is now gated before it publishes.** nfpm builds the `.deb` and `.rpm` in separate passes that can fail independently, and only the `.deb` was smoked — so the `.rpm` shipped on the strength of a different artifact, with every later check reading the published package rather than the built one. `package-smoke-rpm.Dockerfile` reuses the same pinned `rocky-9-compat` image ci.yml already tracks, so the image moves on one schedule rather than under a second Renovate identity. Validated against the real published rc.29 aarch64 rpm: `package smoke PASS: dnf`.

Both invariants are pinned, including one gap neither project had covered — nothing asserted that both formats are smoked, so the `.rpm` gate could have been dropped without anything noticing.
head: refs/pull/152/head
title: Start the matrix when the release is ready, and gate the .rpm before publish

body:
The README is a promise — "tested on every minimum version below" — and nothing checked it. Seven claims had drifted from what any lane actually runs:

- The `.rpm` was never installed on the oldest maintained Fedora, only upgrade-tested from source in the pre-merge ladder. Now a real install lane.
- openSUSE Leap 15.6 was already install-tested while the table named 16.0 as the minimum, understating real coverage.
- Windows is claimed to work; nothing tests it. Now stated plainly rather than implied.
- RHEL and Raspberry Pi OS are named but have no lane — RHEL has no public image to install into, Raspberry Pi OS is Debian 12 underneath. Both are covered by inheritance, and now the README says so.

The invariant that replaces the guesswork parses the support table, resolves the Dockerfile stage graph down from the channel list, and asserts every promised version has a channel that really installs the shipped package on it. Text-searching the Dockerfile was not enough: a pinned-but-unused base looks identical to a tested one, which is exactly the Fedora gap.

Two systems carry no version number, so the parse structurally cannot see them — their disclaimers are pinned separately.

Also fixes a lane that reported success while testing very little: the new Fedora base installed only curl, so `installed-smoke.sh` took its no-openssl branch and skipped every certificate, backup and restore check while still printing PASS.
head: refs/pull/153/head
title: Make the README promises match what is actually tested

body:
The install matrix was the tail of every release. Two changes, measured rather than guessed.

**Both halves now start the same way.** The GitHub matrix triggered on the tag push — the same instant publish starts — and spent ~22 minutes waiting for artifacts that did not exist yet. Unlike the Forgejo case this starved nothing (its runners were free, and every leg started within seconds of the artifacts landing), so it buys no wall clock. It is for consistency: one mechanism starts both halves, and a mechanism that differs per forge is how the two drift apart. `publish.yml` now dispatches both.

**Both Linux legs are sharded.** The channels are independent and were only sequential by default. Measured on a real dispatch against v0.2.0-rc.51: the arm64 leg went from **33 minutes to 7m24s**, four shards balanced at 4m54s / 5m40s / 5m00s / 7m24s. The whole GitHub matrix dropped from 33 to 20 minutes; what remains is macOS **Intel** runners queueing ~15 minutes for capacity, which no workflow change reaches.

Shard counts differ per forge on purpose, the same way `CACHE_CEILING_GB` already does: GitHub gets four, Forgejo gets **two**, because that pool is exactly four self-hosted runners. Four shards there would take all of them — blocking the sibling project’s publish and every PR check — to speed up a leg measured at 8–14 minutes against GitHub’s 20+, which is not the critical path and so would not move the release at all.

An invariant pins the declared shard list against the count handed to the script. Passing four while declaring two would leave half the channels unselected, the shards that ran passing, and the architecture reported green having installed half of what it publishes.

**Note for whoever merges:** the GitHub dispatch needs `Actions: read & write` on `GH_REPO_WRITE_PAT`, which previously held Contents only. The requirement is now documented in `packaging/README.md`. If it is missing the handoff fails loudly within a second rather than silently skipping, and the matrix stays dispatchable by hand with a tag input.

body:
Two gaps behind the same symptom that failed rc.41.

`prerelease.yml` deliberately does NOT call `packaging/push-tag.sh` - it inlines the tag push because that step is where the repo-write PAT reaches shell and the workflow is dispatchable from any branch, so it must not execute a script read back off the checkout. The consequence was that v0.1.22's mirror confirmation never reached the path that actually cuts rcs. The verification half needs no credential, so it goes inline as workflow-defined text: an unauthenticated GET against a slug the runner supplies.

And confirming by HTTP status alone was not enough. An rc number is derived from the source tags, so a name is reusable, and a ref left behind by a partial prune answers 200 while still pointing at the previous release. Both the inline copy and the shared helper now compare the object the mirror serves with the one just pushed (project-standard v0.1.23, vendored here).

The POST is bounded too - unbounded, a stalled sync would have prevented the readback from ever running.

body:
Reproduced on v0.3.0-rc.44: its tap job failed `! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)` because whiskerless rc.65 wrote the shared tap first.

The hazard was already documented at the job - "three jobs write this one repository, and two of them cloning the same tip means the loser pushes a non-fast-forward" - and the mitigation was `concurrency: group: tap-write`. But a concurrency group is scoped to one repository, so it cannot serialise the SIBLING, and both projects publish into `SisyphusMD/homebrew-tap`.

All six writer sites across the two repos (publish.yml pass 1 and pass 2, tap-bottles.yml, in each) now fetch, rebase onto the new tip and retry. Each project renders only its own formula file, so replaying is the correct resolution; a conflict means a genuine collision and still fails loudly.

body:
Rewriting history moves every tag at once, and publish.yml fires on tag pushes, so one rewrite queues one publish run per tag. That happened here today: 35 runs, each rebuilding an already-shipped rc for roughly twenty minutes before the immutable-asset policy refused it on all three hosts.

Nothing was overwritten - that guard did its job - but the refusal is knowable in seconds. This checks whether the tag already has a release before any build starts.

Scoped to `push`, because a dispatch is the documented way to FINISH a partial publish and every helper it runs is idempotent. Read unauthenticated from the mirror, so it needs no secret in a job that deliberately checks out without credentials. Inconclusive answers do not block: a rate-limited probe refusing a legitimate release would be worse than a wasted build, and the immutable-asset refusal is still the backstop.

Exercised against the live API on all four branches - an existing release refuses, an unknown tag proceeds, a stubbed 5xx warns and continues.

body:
Vendors project-standard v0.1.24 and lands the workflow half.

**No unauthenticated GitHub calls.** Unauthenticated github.com allows 60 requests an hour per IP and every runner, mirror probe and CI poller shares one. Several helpers treated their token as optional, so once that budget was gone they did not fail - they answered 403, and the checks built on them stopped deciding anything while still reporting success. push-tag.sh, check-mirror-ci.sh, check-rc-install-matrix.sh, reconcile-releases.sh, github-release.sh and wait-for-release.sh now all make the token mandatory; reconcile also authenticates the asset download, which was going out bare.

push-tag.sh asserts before `git push --atomic`, and prerelease.yml asserts in the push step rather than the mirror step two steps later, because discovering it afterwards leaves the tag published and the run failed.

**The republish guard.** A history rewrite moves every tag at once and publish.yml fires on tag pushes, so one rewrite queues one publish run per tag - 35 of them here, each rebuilding a shipped rc for ~20 minutes before the immutable-asset policy refused it. The guard now checks BOTH publication targets before any build: checking only the source of truth would answer 404 for a partial publish that reached GitHub alone, and let a rewritten tag write new bytes to Forgejo and the NAS before GitHub refused them. It retries a non-definitive answer and then fails closed, since that is precisely when the inconsistency happens; a dispatch with the tag as the ref remains the escape, and is still the way to finish a partial publish.

Exercised against the live forge and mirror: a published tag refuses, an unknown tag proceeds, an unreachable forge and a bad credential both refuse.

body:
Mirror of the whiskerless change. Whiskerless GitHub run 35055059591 stayed red when `brew test` could not resolve rubygems.org on the runner, because the failure landed in our named step and the step-name rule refused the retry.

Vendors project-standard v0.1.25, whose discriminator now reads each failed job's log and retries only when the failed step's own closing lines carry an exact resolver-failure spelling and name a host CI is known to reach. The workflow downloads one log per failed job (`gh api --allow-escape-sequences`, without which `gh` refuses ANSI-coloured bodies) and passes the directory through. The invariant test pins the fetch and the flag.

body:
The build leg has failed on every PR since 2026-09-12 at `apt-get update` inside the Homebrew smoke stage:

```
W: GPG error: https://cli.github.com/packages stable InRelease: NO_PUBKEY 5612B36462313325
E: The repository 'https://cli.github.com/packages stable InRelease' is not signed.
```

The pinned `homebrew/brew` digest is still Docker Hub's latest, so there is nothing to bump to. The image bakes in GitHub's CLI apt source and its keyring at image build time; GitHub rotated the key. The smoke never uses `gh`, so the source is removed before the update rather than re-keyed. Whiskerless's smoke never runs apt in that image, so there is nothing to mirror.

| [ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff) ([source](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff), [changelog](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)) | `0.16.10` → `0.17.0` | ![age](https://developer.mend.io/api/mc/badges/age/pypi/ruff/0.17.0?slim=true) | ![confidence](https://developer.mend.io/api/mc/badges/confidence/pypi/ruff/0.16.10/0.17.0?slim=true) |
| [ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff) ([source](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff), [changelog](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)) | `==0.16.10` → `==0.17.0` | ![age](https://developer.mend.io/api/mc/badges/age/pypi/ruff/0.17.0?slim=true) | ![confidence](https://developer.mend.io/api/mc/badges/confidence/pypi/ruff/0.16.10/0.17.0?slim=true) |

`test_pinned_toolchain_matches_the_lockfile` fails unless pyproject.toml, `uv.lock`, and the workflow literals all name the same version. If this PR is red because Renovate could not relock, run `uv lock` and commit `uv.lock` here.

---

### Release Notes

<details>
<summary>astral-sh/ruff (ruff)</summary>

### [`v0.17.0`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#0170)

[Compare Source](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/compare/0.16.10...0.17.0)

Released on 2026-10-09.

The executables in our macOS and Windows release archives and `ruff` wheels are now code-signed.
macOS executables are signed with an Apple Developer ID certificate and notarized by Apple. Windows
executables have timestamped Authenticode signatures from Azure Artifact Signing. This enables
verification of the release publisher and binary integrity, supports publisher-based allowlisting,
and should reduce security warnings and antivirus false positives.

##### Breaking changes

- Update the default and latest Python versions for 3.15 ([#​28792](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28792))

  Ruff now defaults to Python 3.11 instead of 3.10 when no Python version is configured through
  [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) or
  [`requires-python`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/configuration/#inferring-the-python-version). When
  checking for syntax errors without a configured Python version, Ruff now defaults to Python 3.15
  instead of 3.14.

- Update the default rule set ([#​28786](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28786))

  Several of the `flake8-datetimez` rules
  ([`DTZ001`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/call-datetime-without-tzinfo/),
  [`DTZ005`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/call-datetime-now-without-tzinfo/),
  [`DTZ006`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/call-datetime-fromtimestamp/),
  [`DTZ007`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/call-datetime-strptime-without-zone/),
  [`DTZ011`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/call-date-today/),
  [`DTZ012`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/call-date-fromtimestamp/), and
  [`DTZ901`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/datetime-min-max/)) are no longer enabled by default,
  while [`undefined-local-with-nested-import-star-usage`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/undefined-local-with-nested-import-star-usage/)
  (`F406`), which corresponds to a syntax error, is now enabled by default.

- Update Rust crate quick-junit to 0.8.0 ([#​27295](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/27295))

  JUnit output now uses a `skipped` attribute instead of `disabled` on `<testsuite>` elements and
  includes a `skipped` attribute on the root `<testsuites>` element.

- \[`flake8-import-conventions`] Add `datetime as dt` as a conventional alias (`ICN001`) ([#​28790](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28790))

- Support Unicode dummy variable names ([#​28722](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28722))

  The default [`lint.dummy-variable-rgx`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#lint_dummy-variable-rgx)
  now recognizes underscore-prefixed Unicode names, such as `_次`, as dummy variables.

- Update to Unicode 17 ([#​21229](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/21229), [#​28784](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28784))

  Ruff now uses Unicode 17 data for identifier normalization and named character escapes (`"\N{...}"`).

- Always show unsafe and display-only fixes in the CLI ([#​27810](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/27810))

  The default `full` output format now shows unsafe fixes and suggestions requiring manual review,
  regardless of the [`unsafe-fixes`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#unsafe-fixes) setting.
  Actually applying unsafe fixes still requires explicit opt-in.

- Remove the Python dependency from conda-forge builds ([conda-forge/ruff-feedstock#361](https://github.com/conda-forge/ruff-feedstock/pull/361))

  The conda-forge build no longer depends on Python, now supports linux-riscv64, win-arm64, and
  linux-ppc64le platforms, and now includes shell completions. However, no longer depending on
  Python means that `python -m ruff` and `import ruff` will no longer work. Use `ruff` directly from
  `PATH` instead. PyPI installations and those from the standalone installer are unaffected.

- Remove support for ruff-lsp ([#​28750](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28750))

  Support for `ruff-lsp`, the legacy Python language server [deprecated in Ruff
  v0.9.5](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/releases/tag/0.9.5), has been removed. The Ruff VS Code
  extension now always uses the native language server; `ruff.nativeServer` is deprecated and
  ignored. See the [migration guide](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/editors/migration/).

##### Stabilization

The following rules have been stabilized and are no longer in preview:

- [`lazy-import-mismatch`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/lazy-import-mismatch) (`TID254`)
- [`lazy-import-immediately-resolved`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/lazy-import-immediately-resolved)
  (`TID255`)
- [`os-path-commonprefix`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/os-path-commonprefix) (`RUF071`)

The following behaviors have been stabilized:

- The formatter, [`unsorted-imports`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/unsorted-imports/) (`I001`),
  [`line-too-long`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/line-too-long/) (`E501`), and
  [`doc-line-too-long`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/doc-line-too-long/) (`W505`) now
  consistently ignore trailing pragma comments when computing line length. This resolved several
  bugs involving interactions between these rules
  ([#​27313](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/27313)) but may also cause existing imports to be
  reformatted and was thus classified as a breaking change.

##### Preview features

- \[`flake8-bugbear`] Report the method name and a more precise range (`B005`) ([#​27050](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/27050))
- \[`refurb`] Mark fix unsafe and move to `suspicious` (`FURB152`) ([#​28405](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28405))
- \[`ruff`] Allow docstrings in strict mode (`RUF067`) ([#​28679](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28679))

##### Bug fixes

- \[`flake8-builtins`] Expand checks in class scopes (`A001`) ([#​29076](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29076))
- \[`flake8-self`] Allow private access on `object.__new__(cls)` instances (`SLF001`) ([#​29001](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29001))
- \[`flake8-tidy-imports`] Skip `lazy-import-mismatch` in stubs (`TID254`) ([#​29095](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29095))
- \[`flake8-type-checking`] Add the notion of runtime-ambiguous references ([#​26508](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/26508))
- \[`flake8-type-checking`] Never flag annotations in function scopes ([#​29183](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29183))
- \[`pyflakes`] Mark the fix as unsafe when it creates a docstring (`F541`) ([#​28258](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28258))
- \[`pylint`] Preserve trailing comments in `useless-return` fix (`PLR1711`) ([#​29180](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29180))
- \[`ruff`] Avoid false positive when `pytest.raises` is used in a `with` statement (`RUF061`) ([#​28186](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28186))

- \[`pyupgrade`] Suggest `typing.TypeForm` on Python 3.15 (`UP035`) ([#​29084](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29084))

Hypfer/Valetudo ### [`v2026.10.0`](https://github.com/Hypfer/Valetudo/releases/tag/2026.10.0): Valetudo 2026.10.0 [Compare Source](https://github.com/Hypfer/Valetudo/compare/2026.08.0...2026.10.0)

2026.10.0

New robots, new Fab ##### Valetudo 2026.10.0 I have spent a lot of time working on Valetudo, without working directly on Valetudo. While wrapping up, I saw that the first commit for the new bots was in *march*. So, what changed? 1. We now have two modern MOVA robots that can run Valetudo in the same "it just works" way as always. 2. We also now have the Dustfab, which is the spiritual successor of the Dustbuilder, where I rewrote the thing (but not in Rust) to clean up 8 years of technical debt. 3. Lastly, we now have a new and improved Fastboot rooting flow (for the second time this year), using a helper binary that just does the right thing, packaged up in a way that is even easier to use. ... and on top, the Midea implementation should be more stable now. ##### The Dustfab As you may have heard in the news, we have a severe global fab shortage. Two releases ago, I've said that the new bots were blocked by infra. So, I had to unblock that first, and to do that, eight years of technical debt, caused by a research prototype being put into production, had to be dealt with. This was (you might've already guessed it) "accelerated" by AI, in the sense that I told it to do 5 things, of which it did three, one of them with three layers of neurotic caches just in case. So it still took quite some screaming and a while. But now it is done. The new thing - Doesn't use E-Mail anymore - Reacts faster - Microservices (are they still cool?) - Gives more feedback - Is easier to maintain - Docker (state-of-the-art (in 2015)) - Has a modern (wtf does that even mean) design - Is dishwasher-safe - Has cool captchas - Cleans up previously confusing historically-grown wording - Also is the new and improved checker and, most importantly, comes with even more of my opinions. I think you're gonna like it. I do like it very much. \=> [fab.valetudo.cloud](https://fab.valetudo.cloud) Moving this architecture under my roof also means that people should please stop pestering Dennis with nonsense. He cannot help you. There is no point in wasting the time of that very busy and highly capable man with seven consecutive emails about.. I honestly don't even know what. Seriously though, it makes zero sense to have someone on a level like him be bombarded with consumer spam, so now people can only bombard me, which I will nullroute. ##### The robots It's MOVA. Surprise. I had high hopes for Midea, but.. I mean they're alright-ish, but coming from a market-leading brand like Dreame, one did wonder why one would pay more for less. So now we have some MOVAs, which is the more budget-brand spin-off of Dreame, where they mostly recycle previous-gen components of Dreame into new bots. But also sometimes not? It is all very confusing. These robots are based on a new platform, however, with the new and improved flow, that detail (and the friction and risks of it) should be pretty much invisible. It was however very much not invisible while building up to this point. You're welcome. I'd like to place a huge thank you to an anonymous collaborator here, who just showed up out of nowhere and had fun rooting new robots. Simply for the fun of "I'm gonna conquer this thing". Your work/thoughts helped (and continues to help) a lot, but, more importantly, just seeing someone hacking for the fun of hacking did *so much* for my morale. ##### Mova V50 I have to admit I really like this robot. The first time I saw it at someone else's place, I just thought "wow, nice". Primarily, I think that is due to the new wheels (which I think premiered on the X50? Not sure), that are - effectively - silent. Picture having seen probably over a hundred different vaccum robot models over the years with them all making similar-ish noises, and that guy just suddenly doesn't. So that was cool. The rest of it is more of what we had on older dreames, but improved. It can limit the max charge. It can now leap over higher thresholds. It can fit under lower furniture. Haptics are good. The dock has a shape that is much better suited for a lot of spaces. It's a good bot. I like it, and have been using it since march. ##### Mova Z60 I have to admit I don't really like this bot. I bought it both out of curiosity and out of thinking that you people would likely be very happy with a roller mop with Valetudo support. I kinda regret doing so. But by the time regret set in, I had already voided its warranty, so here we are. It is the V50 but worse. It is thicker, louder, more annoying and has a glossy dock. The mop not only needs longer drying times but also constantly cycles its motor on and off during cleaning, which is an infuriating noise that annoys me two floors away. The benefit I guess is supposed to be somewhat better mopping, but, honestly, I don't see it? At least not with my needs. Maybe people with pets will see some value in it. Either way, compromises were made, and I do not think that they were worth it. But now there's a Valetudo-supported modern roller-mop-equipped bot. > \[!NOTE] > **Editor-Hypfer:** > While wrapping up the release, I wanted to update the Amazon reflinks in the docs. > Amazon did *not* let me generate a reflink for this one, as, apparently, too many people have returned it to them. So that's a datapoint. > > Of course, in true big-tech fashion, their wording is that I should *consider* linking something else. And then they hide the button. So you simply *can't* link it no matter if you consider or not. > Corporate speak truly is a crime against humanity. Words have meanings. AGI 😭 ##### What's next in robots? Truth be told, I kinda hate putting this here, but I also know that people's brains have been fried, so that an announcement of two new things will always be met with "okay, what about thing 3 to n"? They don't say n of course, as that is weird nerd lingo. Anyway, I do not know. While I'd (as always) like to look into more robots, most of the new ones still.. kinda suck? I'm just looking at them, thinking "no, I'm not paying money for that and certainly not the price you expect me to pay for it". And you should feel the same, honestly. I am observing the market and how prices and availability develops, but the X40 was fine, and, now that new availability of it has gotten a bit limited, the V50 is fine. What else could anyone possibly want. And why. While building Dustfab, for testing, I've picked up my Roborock S5 Max (2019) again, and gave it another spin. Turns out that it's a perfectly fine vacuum robot, that gives you like 70% of what one of those 1500€ models would give you, but for.. idk like 30€ used? Of course, buying used is not for everyone (me often included, tbh), but.. seriously just look at the market. Oh and look at the recession we're in. ##### The fixes As I am an idiot, I gave AI a spin to figure out why on Midea, Valetudo's phoenix failsafe sometimes has to kick in due to too much memory usage. So it spent a few hours doing.. whatever, with me just watching. Eventually culminating in the AI rambling on about creating context and something about an S3 plan... which must've been a hallucination, given that we're running locally. Anyway, Valetudo now reuses created TLS contexts, which may or may not fix that. It's kinda hard to reproduce unfortunately. Additionally, the MQTT interface has been cleaned up and rid of unnecessary optionality. And, lastly, the forced garbage collection logic has received some new thought after many years. This should in many situations lead to lower CPU usage and better performance. ##### Closing thoughts This.. took a while. As said further up, work started at the beginning of this year. As you could perhaps slightly see, it was a fractal of work, where every work item was actually more work items. On top, the daily grind happens, life happens, real work happens, real world happens. One important thing to put here is that the new robots are somewhat less forgiving, in the sense that you have to pull the battery if you mess up - an action that requires destruction of warranty seals. I did spend a lot of time improving the tooling there to prevent that, but the risk is still greater than on older bots. So there's that. If you're curious what exactly "new tooling" means, check out the rewritten rooting instructions in the docs. ##### The usual If you like this release or Valetudo in general, and/or you want me to look at more bots, you might want to consider donating: ##### Autogenerated changelog ##### Features - **vendor.dreame**: Map roller mop fluffer consumable and ignore the rest for now [`2e832db`](http://github.com/Hypfer/Valetudo/commit/2e832dbddca4f65ee4d1c1e5a99840019f832ea1) - **vendor.dreame**: Mova V50/Z60 [`c0987f0`](http://github.com/Hypfer/Valetudo/commit/c0987f0b6c87d3f542db2d1ce3a0c6c6913ccc2d) - Some logo variants [`e048f8f`](http://github.com/Hypfer/Valetudo/commit/e048f8f10879b093de0bbeccfb0cb0d0624c43a7) - **ui**: Add another spectator map pip window size [`4ca5609`](http://github.com/Hypfer/Valetudo/commit/4ca5609490b9cd85cfa2b25d4a808ccca109658a) ##### Fixes - **mqtt**: Remove legacy cruft homie and home assistant optionality [`31bbc50`](http://github.com/Hypfer/Valetudo/commit/31bbc50c8dc34d02d4ed1a24d2febe0444344c64) - **core**: Improve forced gc condition [`40e767d`](http://github.com/Hypfer/Valetudo/commit/40e767deb3607ece9b36e0af1643e59fdd1f270d) -
